pr_title: Support Enumerator::Lazy in where clause filters.
pr_body:
### Summary
If we assume we have a Post record with an ID of 1, before this change the result of this would be 0.

```ruby
    Post.where(id: [1].lazy).count
```

Whereas now it will return a value of 1.

Fixes #41089.

Thank you for the pull request but I don't think it makes sense to complicate the implementation of the framework to support this. As a developer you know the enumerator you get is lazy, since you created it.

In your real case example, you can change the code from:

```ruby
posts = Post.find_each.lazy.select(&:some_method)
comments = Comment.where(post: posts)
```

to

```ruby
posts = Post.find_each.lazy.select(&:some_method)
comments = Comment.where(post: posts.to_a)
```

issue_context.title: Using a lazy enumerator in ActiveRecord's where method returns no results
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce
Use a lazy enumerator in conjunction with ActiveRecord's `where` method. A query that would return results with a non-lazy equivalent will return nothing when the lazy enumerator is used.

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  git_source(:github) { |repo| "https://github.com/#{repo}.git" }

  # Activate the gem you are reporting the issue against.
  gem "activerecord", "6.1.0"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_lazy_enumerator_in_where_clause
    5.times { Post.create! }
    ids = Post.pluck(:id)
    assert_equal Post.where(id: ids).count, Post.where(id: ids.lazy).count
  end
end
```

To give a real-world example of why this may be an issue — consider a situation where we need to filter a collection of objects using Ruby and then use those filtered results in another query. To avoid loading all of the initial objects in memory we might do `find_each.lazy`:

```ruby
posts = Post.find_each.lazy.select(&:some_method)
comments = Comment.where(post: posts)
```

In this case, `comments` would be empty even if the `select` block returned a non-empty result and there were comments that belong to the resultant posts.

### Expected behavior
When using the result of a lazy enumerator as a condition in the `where` statement the result should be the same as it's non-lazy equivalent.

### Actual behavior
The results are different.

### System configuration
**Rails version**: 6.1.0

**Ruby version**: ruby 2.6.6p146 (2020-03-31 revision 67876) [x86_64-darwin19]

review_comments:
Not sure (yet) if maintainers accept this behavior change, it probably need to adapt the way it re-assigns the `opts` local variable. Instead of create two hashes on the double iteration, use `each_with_object`:

```suggestion
          opts = opts.each_with_object do |(key, value), hash|
            key = key.to_s
            hash[klass.attribute_aliases[key] || key] = value.is_a?(Enumerator::Lazy) ? value.to_a : value
          end
```
Could you use use a map to avoid iterating twice?
